title: Cell enlargement, polarity competition and migration persistence
subtitle: Working manuscript outline with revised figures, complete retained supplements and explicit scientific qualifications
stage: Completed round-2 Figures 2–4, including approved Holmes follow-up
overview: Working hypothesis: WGD-associated enlargement changes how established polarity is organized and replaced; these changes may provide a physical basis for greater migration persistence. The theoretical contribution tests size under unchanged local kinetic parameters. Length differs between model cells to represent WGD-associated enlargement, rather than elongation during a turn. Existing migration observations supply empirical motivation; new paired WGD motility results retain a substantial, explicitly reserved contribution.

Enlarged cells resist imposed replacement through distinct initiation, spatial and temporal response signatures (Figure 2). Distance between competing regions matters only at short range; enlarged cells resist replacement and resolve coexistence slowly mainly because of size itself (Figure 3). Spring's middle size is the supported exception in which extra accessible separation adds a substantial resolution-time contribution. Enlarged cells hold heading longer under fluctuating input — at or above the geometric expectation at weak input — and the advantage declines as input strengthens. (Figure 4). Geometry and multiple-front fractions are descriptive: erosion below the single-front geometric expectation can also occur while a single front persists. Observed migration summaries, conditional OU velocity-memory estimates and simulated polarity-heading readouts remain separate evidence.

This is a working manuscript outline. Figures 1 and 5 and the reserved Figure 6 experimental section retain their preceding content. Activity polarity, modelled replacement, observed migration and conditional OU velocity memory remain distinct readouts; their biological connection is an experimental hypothesis.

sections.title: Figure 1. Enlargement changes the cue duration required for lasting polarity replacement
sections.role: Comparative theoretical foundation: five established models, three finite challenges, and two distinct scalar replacement gates.

assets.caption: Current canonical comparison, 10 October Spearman revision; corrected independent-endpoint deBelly.
assets.page_title: Figure 1. Five models and three finite challenges

legend: A, Example wave-pinning preparation from a homogeneous state using a finite left patch. The cue ends at 0.773 native time units, whereas the subsequent basal relaxation establishes the polarized profile later (reported establishment arrival about 116). Coloured profiles and orientation samples distinguish input duration from autonomous development. The grey late interval is verification, not additional stimulation. Profiles are scaled for display.

B, Three rightward finite challenges restart the identical qualifying nominal-amplitude, relative-20% basal checkpoint at each model and length: fixed physical support 3 (Spring 0.2 native length units), relative support 20%, and a linear ramp with constant physical slope. Patch peaks remain fixed within each model; a fixed-slope ramp has a larger peak in a longer domain. Goryachev patches use the independently selected, length-independent multiplier K=64 (peak 6.4), which makes this a response-permissive comparison rather than a calibrated equal biochemical dose across models.

C, Spearman rank correlation between length and the shortest tested passing pulse duration, separately for orientation replacement and strength replacement, across Wave-pinning, Goryachev, corrected deBelly, Holmes 3 and Spring. Each cell reports the correlation and included successful-length count. All audited scalar successes enter, including those failing the separate native-field tail criterion. At least four distinct successful lengths and nonconstant durations are required; censored and preparation-ineligible cases receive no invented time. The companion duration curves retain all lengths and field-status markers.

After each positive pulse, input returns to the native basal value for 10,000 native time units. Orientation requires all 201 final-500 samples to have scalar orientation above 0.05 and contrast at least 0.05, with orientation range below 0.005. Strength additionally requires every tail orientation to be within 1% of the absolute initial leftward scalar orientation; it does not compare individual pole heights or amounts. The separate native-field tail flag requires pointwise range and projected 500-unit drift within 0.1% of frozen field scales. The reported duration excludes preparation and recovery. It is the shortest passing tested duration, with sampled fail/pass boundaries refined to 1%; narrower unobserved intervals are not excluded.

deBelly uses independently commanded corrected endpoints, rather than the deprecated in-loop centered extension. Spring length and time retain native units and are not silently converted to micrometres or seconds. Model-specific axes and stimulus definitions prevent interpreting cross-model amplitudes or clocks as biologically calibrated equivalents.
narrative: Fixed-width and relative-width patches show perfectly increasing rank order among observed successes in Wave-pinning, Goryachev, Holmes 3 and Spring; enlargement often increases the finite stimulation required for a retained response.

The response depends on the cue geometry and model. Spring has a negative constant-slope association (Spearman correlation -0.874 for both gates), while Holmes orientation under the constant-slope cue is nearly unassociated with length (0.047).
Corrected deBelly curves are nonmonotone despite moderate positive rank correlations. The full duration curves and eligibility ranges are essential to the result.
These are deterministic polarity-replacement experiments. They motivate, but do not measure, spontaneous polarity memory or migration persistence.
measurements: Mechanism-linked cellular follow-up would match local input support, amplitude and duration, track the original and challenged activity regions through stimulation and withdrawal, and distinguish orientation replacement from recovered activity strength. This validation is proposed and has no experimental results in this outline.
limitations: Correlations are conditional on observed scalar success, rather than an unbiased summary of all possible sizes or a universal scaling law. Ineligible starts are distinct from responses unobserved by the finite horizon.

A retained scalar response can coexist with a changing native field. Only 13 of the 72 corrected deBelly scalar successes pass the separate native-field tail flag. Resolution checks from the earlier centered-deBelly campaign cannot qualify the corrected replacement thresholds.

sections.title: Figure 2. Replacement resistance in enlarged cells arises through three mechanism classes; cue shape and timing distinguish their signatures
sections.role: Distinguish replacement-resistance mechanisms using initiation, equal-area cue widths and measured pulse/gap retention.

assets.caption: Figure 2 round2 with completed Holmes retention
assets.page_title: Figure 2. Shape and timing distinguish mechanism classes

legend: Enlarged cells resist replacement through distinct initiation, cue-width and gap-retention signatures, supporting three mechanism classes in the deterministic cue assays.

A, Incumbent amount, extent and peak across the retained 97 states. B, Initiation normalized to each model’s L19 value at central area and the fixed 10% L19 reporter threshold. Brackets propagate saved-sample intervals. deBelly L19 and L39 initiation both lie in (0, 0.5] native units; its normalized ratio is unavailable. Its separate native-time inset places open downward triangles at the measured upper bounds 0.5 and at the actual lengths 19 and 39, with arrows toward smaller times.

C, Narrow/broad replacement-time ratio at fixed commanded spatial area. Open triangles and arrows are one-sided bounds; question marks denote uninformative ratios. Wave-pinning has a growing large penalty. Holmes grows from about 29 at L19 to above 133 at L23; growth through L39 is unresolved because both width arms are censored. Goryachev and Spring have modest penalties rather than exact width invariance. Commanded area is not calibrated photon dose.

D, Four equal pulses with total ON 1.5 times the model-length commitment calibration; final D after recovery is the colour. For Holmes L31, L35 and L39, diamonds identify the last inter-pulse gap-end D from the targeted L27-referenced protocol; this endpoint is distinct from final fate. Gap0 uses the zero-duration boundary after the third pulse. No continuous commitment by 100,000 at these three lengths is extreme finite-horizon replacement resistance. Crosses preserve failed field tails, including 31 of the 36 deBelly fate cells.

E, L39 gap4 histories. Shading marks cue ON; circles and squares mark pulse and gap endpoints. The deBelly trace includes full recovery to its measured final fate; other traces show through one pulse duration of recovery, with full post-recovery D stated in each plot. Holmes retains more than 84% of raw challenger share through all three gaps, although D is slightly negative in the first two and final D remains below 0.5. Retention of share differs from the secondary S3 criterion requiring D at least zero. F, The class table has a numerical evidence row for every model and signature; membership is unchanged. deBelly early collapse and final replacement survive its separate quarter-step check, while later-gap timing and endpoint fields remain sensitive. All native kinetics are unchanged. These polarity readouts are distinct from observed migration and conditional OU persistence.

The separate Holmes L39 gap16 transfer has heterogeneous bounded input during gaps: S3 successes are 8/12, 9/12, 10/12 after gaps 1–3. Raw share ratios span 0.02152–1.78070; final D spans -0.063410–0.999944. Ten of twelve noisy histories replace, while matched-mean and zero controls do not. The class table describes gaps without added input; this separate transfer demonstrates variable retention and fate under spatially heterogeneous input.
narrative: Enlarged cells resist replacement through distinct initiation, cue-width and gap-retention signatures, supporting three mechanism classes in the deterministic cue assays.
The targeted Holmes measurements report activity at every pulse and gap endpoint, independently of eventual replacement.
No continuous commitment by 100,000 at Holmes L31, L35 and L39 is a finite-horizon finding of extreme replacement resistance.
measurements: Vary physical cue support at fixed commanded spatial input area and measure time to eligible75% challenger activity share.
Apply equal-total-ON pulse trains, measure activity share at every pulse and gap endpoint, then report postwithdrawal fate and field stability independently.
limitations: deBelly normalized initiation unresolved within first-update intervals
Holmes width-penalty growth through L39 uninformative; moderate-length growth verified
deBelly later-gap timing and endpoint fields remain numerically sensitive
Holmes share retention is distinct from S3 D>=0 retention success and from commitment
Modest Goryachev/Spring width penalties qualify binary no-penalty wording; no class change
Selected mechanistic signatures do not causally allocate replacement resistance

Bounded heterogeneous Holmes gap input gives S3 successes 8/12, 9/12, 10/12; some histories lose share or replace, unlike deterministic/mean controls. Integrated gap exposure is 2.46 times ON exposure; deterministic class membership does not imply universal noisy-gap retention.

sections.title: Figure 3. Separation slows the resolution of coexisting regions at short range; at matched separation, cell size dominates both driven takeover and resolution.
sections.role: Separate matched-gap size effects from extra accessible separation for driven handover and cue-free resolution.
sections.purpose: Existing-output recomposition and interval-safe decomposition without model retuning.

assets.caption: Separation slows the resolution of coexisting regions at short range; at matched separation, cell size dominates both driven takeover and resolution.
assets.page_title: Figure 3. Separation slows the resolution of coexisting regions at short range; at matched separation, cell size dominates both driven takeover and resolution.

legend: Separation slows the resolution of coexisting regions at short range; at matched separation, cell size dominates both driven takeover and resolution. Times and gaps use native units.

A. A native cue is rotated at fixed cell size. The initial gap runs from the incumbent 10%-contrast edge to the cue support near edge. The inset holds the physical gap at 4 across small and large Wave-pinning rings; changing native widths also changes center separation. A1 measures continuous-cue complete-region handover. B withdraws the cue at complete-region challenger/incumbent excess ratio 1 and measures the first single resolved peak.

B. Left: Goryachev continuous-cue histories at circumference 37.8 and gaps 2 and 8; white dashed lines mark native continuous handover roots. Right: Wave-pinning at circumference 47.6, measured withdrawal gaps 2.78 and 14.84; the near condition resolves within 1140–1160, while the far condition remains unresolved through 20,000. Colour scales are shared within each model; the different assay time windows are shown explicitly. Native species are active chemical species. These maps display fields, not cell trajectories.

C. Goryachev handover rises with gap, whereas Holmes is nearly flat. Wave-pinning and Spring rise near the edge and then plateau; Wave-pinning does have a distance effect. Open circles are borderline placements. An × at the axis floor denotes an unavailable genuine two-region handover, not a time estimate. Size is consistently encoded by lightness and line style. The coloured top ticks mark initial antipodal-placement gaps.

D. Equal-amount cue-free resolution rises steeply at short range: approximately gaps 0–5 in Wave-pinning, 2–5.5 in Holmes, and 0.2–0.7 in Spring (the transition shifts with size). Thereafter observed curves flatten or remain unresolved. Holmes has 12/23 eligible ratio-1 main-curve times censored. The nine approved Holmes continuations to 80,000 resolve six histories; three middle-size histories remain unresolved at 80,000. Other Holmes lower bounds retain 20,000. These mixed horizons do not establish a downturn with gap. Unresolved times use open triangles and upward arrows; finite brackets use intervals, and lines do not bridge censored or ineligible placements. Top ticks mark each size's measured withdrawal gap in the initial-antipodal-cue trajectory; they do not assert exactly antipodal withdrawal centers. Goryachev includes a nonmonotone near-edge response. All alternate, merged and unseeded cases remain in the CSV and original native reader.

E. Each larger size is compared with the smallest size at the largest shared measured gap, using piecewise-linear interpolation inside measured support. Solid bars represent size at matched gap; hatched bars represent extra separation to the larger-size antipodal-placement endpoint. Bars give log₁₀ time ratios; finite B interval limits are marked. Open-ended bars retain one-sided bounds. A question mark means both relevant times are censored and the ratio is indeterminate. Such bars cannot be stacked into a measured total. Total ratios and all interpolation sources are tabulated separately. Size at matched gap dominates driven handover in all four models and the identifiable cue-free comparisons. Extra separation adds at most 1.15× for driven handover and about 1.01–1.07× in resolved Wave-pinning/Goryachev cue-free comparisons; Spring middle size is the supported exception (1.75×), with a larger matched-gap size term (4.29×). After extension, the Holmes middle-size matched-gap term is ≥2.37; its large-size term is only ≥0.618 and does not establish a positive size effect. Holmes extra-separation terms remain indeterminate. Enlarged cells' access to farther separations therefore does not generally explain their slower resolution.

The complete translation page, earlier main plate, all three B seeding ratios, A2 pulse brackets, 50%-edge reclassification, direct heading checks and numerical controls remain in the supplement and original reader. The finer-mesh Goryachev B ratio-1 gap-4 comparison has about 4% resolution-time sensitivity. Finite horizons establish lower bounds rather than permanent arrest; scalar/spatial fate and native-field stationarity are separate. The only new simulations are the nine approved Holmes cue-free continuations; no model retuning is included. Simulated activity heading, observed migration and conditional OU persistence remain distinct.
narrative: Separation slows the resolution of coexisting regions at short range; at matched separation, cell size dominates both driven takeover and resolution. Times and gaps use native units.
At matched separation, size dominates both driven takeover and cue-free resolution. Extra separation contributes substantially in the supported Spring middle-size exception.
The nine approved Holmes continuations extend the original exact endpoints to 80,000; unresolved conditions remain lower bounds and ratios of two censored times remain indeterminate.
The Holmes large-size matched-gap lower bound is below one and does not establish a positive large-size effect; the full qualification is retained in the legend and decomposition CSV.
measurements: Measure complete-region continuous-cue handover against initial edge gap at fixed circumference.
Withdraw at challenger/incumbent excess ratio 1 and measure first single-region resolution against the actual withdrawal gap.
Decompose size at matched gap and extra separation using interpolation only within measured support; propagate censoring and saved-sample brackets.
limitations: Censored ratios remain bounds or indeterminate; no horizon point substitution.
Nine approved Holmes extensions completed; three still censored at 80,000. Other cases retain 20,000. Holmes large-size matched-gap bound does not establish a positive size effect.
claims: Separation response depends on the model and on whether competition is externally driven or cue-free.
Goryachev has a stronger continuous-cue handover distance response than Holmes 3 over valid external two-region placements.
Measured global heading qualifies the proposed geometry-only persistence translation; complete-region handover is typically near half the requested angle.
sections.mechanistic_scope: Fixed-size rotation isolates separation from changes in size, incumbent extent and pool size. The observed responses constrain mechanism classes, but are not a kinetic-term ablation, molecular-transport measurement or unique causal identification.

sections.title: Figure 4. Enlarged cells hold heading longer under fluctuating input — at or above the geometric expectation at weak input — and the advantage declines as input strengthens.
sections.role: Measure the heading decay-rate advantage and describe geometric normalization and spatial organization under fluctuating input.
legend: Enlarged cells hold heading longer under fluctuating input — at or above the geometric expectation at weak input — and the advantage declines as input strengthens. The geometric statement describes model-specific weakest measurable point estimates: f = 0.003 for Wave-pinning and Holmes, and f = 0.0003–0.001 for Spring. Confidence intervals also admit sub-geometric gains in Holmes and Spring. At the shared displayed input f = 0.003, Spring is already below its actual geometric expectation (rate ratio 7.55 versus geometry 8.55), while its large-cell regime is still classified as single front. (A) Native activity kymographs for small and large Wave-pinning and Holmes at f = 0.003, plus a large Wave-pinning example at f = 0.1; width is proportional to circumference, with shared activity scales within each model. (B) Heading autocorrelation at f = 0.003 on model-specific logarithmic ordinates with whole-seed 95% bootstrap bands; intervals extending below zero continue beyond the positive plotting range. (C) Small/large rotational decay-rate ratio at the shortest usable lag satisfying the frozen lag rule, with pointwise 95% CIs. Reference lines show unity and nominal single-front geometry (9); actual-circumference normalization is reported in the supplement. Marker fill describes the large-cell regime; squares flag non-exponential lag dependence. (D) Multiple-front fractions with bootstrap intervals, reported descriptively: Holmes and Spring can fall below geometry while still single-front, so these data do not establish multiple fronts as the cause of erosion. (E) Fixed-reference-lag noise tolerance increases with size; smallest/largest CIs separate in all three shown models. Small cells are lighter solid, large cells darker dotted. Native units are used. Post hoc H1 amendment: evaluate gains and supported reversals only at inputs strictly below the point estimate of the largest cell’s own f½; strict CI and size noise-tolerance rules are unchanged. Both main-view observation arms pass the amended H1 overall, while frozen rate H1 is inconclusive in both; all calls appear alongside in S0. H2/H3/A6 τ gates are retired. Goryachev is excluded from the main because its ratios derive from forced or non-exponential conditions, and remains complete in the supplement. Simulated polarity heading is distinct from migration persistence and conditional OU estimates.
narrative: Enlarged cells hold heading longer under fluctuating input — at or above the geometric expectation at weak input — and the advantage declines as input strengthens.
Post hoc H1 passes in both main-view observation arms; frozen rate H1 remains inconclusive. All seven views, both arms and both forcing choices remain alongside in S0.
Geometry and multiple-front fractions are descriptive. The data do not establish multiple fronts as the cause of the declining advantage.
measurements: Use endpoint coverage R ≥ 0.1 and a whole-seed bootstrap. Select the shortest usable lag at which small-cell autocorrelation is at most 0.98; report every usable lag and flag drift greater than 1.5-fold.
Measure fixed-reference-lag noise tolerance at autocorrelation 0.5 across every designed input, using log-input interpolation and explicit bounds.
Normalize the rate ratio by actual mean-circumference geometry, relative to the single-front expectation; this is not site diffusivity.
limitations: The H1 domain restriction to inputs below the largest size's estimated noise tolerance is post hoc.
Weak-input geometric comparisons describe point estimates; Holmes and Spring confidence intervals also admit sub-geometric gains.
Non-exponential lags, forcing, off-grid lags and nonpositive autocorrelations remain explicit. Goryachev is complete in the supplement.
H2, H3 and A6 tau-based gates are retired; their frozen historical calls are preserved for provenance.
Simulated activity-heading persistence is distinct from observed migration and conditional OU persistence estimates.

sections.title: Figure 5. Published migration summaries support a persistence hypothesis with conditional OU interpretation
sections.role: Existing empirical support, with observed migration summaries kept separate from fitted velocity-memory parameters.

assets.caption: Reassembled Figure 5: original A and C–F numerical evidence, revised MSD/curve-shape panel B.
assets.page_title: Figure 5. Migration observations and conditional OU interpretation

assets.caption: Figure 5B continued: enlarged detail with explicit raster-sample caveat.
assets.page_title: Figure 5. Migration observations and conditional OU interpretation

legend: A, Published/digitized enlarged or polyploid-group to reference-group ratios for nine migration summaries, alongside primary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) fit predictions. Xuan contributes sampled mean speed and population mean-squared displacement (MSD) at the last shared lag, approximately 10.95 h; Hosny summaries are group medians. Mallin central-bar statistic is not specified by the source and retains the historical mean approximation. These distinct source summaries are not interchangeable measures of persistence.

B, Upper: twelve chosen display samples from each digitized Xuan population MSD curve (small points) and the unchanged fitted analytical OU expectation (solid lines), on logarithmic lag and MSD axes. These are samples of the published raster curves, not recovered experimental lag positions or independent cell observations; the original experimental lag grid is unknown. The open circle identifies the crossover of the full digitized traces at approximately 2.32 h, computed by linear interpolation in native lag and MSD. The open diamond identifies the different fitted OU crossover at approximately 1.11 h. Lower: descriptive slopes of log(MSD) versus log(lag) fitted in six equal log-lag windows of the full digitized curves (points), and matching-window moving OU slopes (solid lines). Each window spans approximately 0.304 decades; both observed and model slopes use the same full window support. Observed raster columns remain correlated and give no biological sample size or confidence interval. These slopes are newly calculated curve-shape summaries, not author-reported local exponents or fitted OU memory times. A constant power-law exponent would appear horizontal; reference values 1 and 2 indicate diffusive and straight-line scaling. The model does not reproduce the complete observed curvature or the observed crossover. The analytical fit, all fitting targets and numerical inputs to A and C–F are unchanged.

C, Representative Xuan primary-fit model-generated tracks, with sampled speed, total path length and directness (net displacement divided by path length). Both groups use identical spatial scales. The tracks are simulations, not published individual-cell trajectories; a slower sampled trajectory can nevertheless have greater endpoint directness. Dashed chords illustrate the contribution of finite-time displacements.

D, With reference-group parameters fixed, vary enlarged-group persistence and velocity-noise ratios. Separate surfaces show change in the descriptive data-misfit score and in the total regularized objective; the selected fit and equal-group reference are marked. The heuristic score is not a calibrated likelihood, and the surfaces are not confidence regions.

E, Primary paired persistence and velocity-noise estimates for Xuan 2018, Mallin 2023, Jemaà 2017, Jemaà 2023 and the Hosny hypoxic baseline. F, Enlarged/reference persistence folds under the primary 10-minute prior, 5- and 20-minute alternatives and stronger/weaker pooling, with the pooled geometric mean. Priors and pooling define conditional sensitivity scenarios, not uncertainty intervals. The Jemaà comparisons constrain speed alone, leaving persistence/noise tradeoffs dependent on hierarchy and priors.

The fitted population contrasts span stable tetraploids, giant polyploids and treatment-induced polyaneuploid cancer cells (PACCs). The inherited WGD+/WGD− labels in the artwork are comparison shorthand and do not establish matched WGD-only interventions in every study. Hosny observations derive from the recovered preprint; equivalence to the journal version remains unresolved.
narrative: Xuan combines lower sampled speed (0.64-fold) with greater late-lag population MSD (2.08-fold); Mallin combines shorter path length (0.52-fold) with greater directness (3.12-fold). Persistence-related behaviour therefore deserves analysis separately from speed.
Hosny baseline PACCs have greater median path length (1.77-fold) and directness (1.67-fold). Signed migration index is a separate directional summary.

All five primary OU comparisons infer longer velocity memory. The pooled primary persistence fold is about 15.8, and remains above one across the declared prior/pooling scenarios; this is a conditional model result.

The fit does not reproduce the complete Xuan curve shape within its raster envelope, and data-only sensitivity has rank 18 of 22. Optimization completion does not establish model adequacy or uniquely identified persistence times.

The observed Xuan curves cross near 2.32 h while the unchanged fitted OU curves cross near 1.11 h. Matched-window slopes make the remaining curve-shape discrepancy visible; fitted persistence is a conditional summary.
Lower sampled speed can coexist with greater late-lag displacement in the enlarged-group comparison. Its causal connection to polarity mechanisms requires matched activity and migration measurements.
measurements: The new WGD assay should measure matched trajectories directly, with declared sampling and observation duration, and assess speed, displacement, directness and lag-dependent MSD before considering fitted persistence. An activity-polarity memory measurement would complement these quantities without equating activity and velocity.
limitations: Neither these heterogeneous group comparisons nor the OU fits establish that enlargement alone causes persistence. Cell identity, induction/treatment and acquisition differences require explicit treatment in the new experiments.

The requested observed-point/model-line and curve-shape display is implemented. The original experimental lag grid remains unknown; neither display samples nor raster-derived slopes supply independent biological replicates. The observed/model crossover discrepancy remains visible.

legend: A, Proposed experimental context: the SUM-159 chemically induced WGD+/− pair is the agreed starting pilot with the Speros collaboration. Imaging should first be optimized for that pair before expansion to additional cell lines. Ploidy/group identity, physical size and morphology need to be documented so the intended comparison is clear.

B, Reserved for representative experimental fields and trajectories under the selected acquisition conditions. The eventual panel should state sampling interval, usable duration, spatial scale, track eligibility and exclusions. Number of independent preparations and biological replicates remains to be specified.

C, Reserved for empirical motility summaries: sampled speed, accumulated path length, endpoint displacement/directness and lag-dependent MSD. The final readouts, follow-up window and analysis plan are to be settled before interpreting the data; this placeholder does not imply that all listed measurements will be technically feasible.

D, Reserved for the measured relationship between WGD-associated enlargement and migration behaviour, including size distributions and controls needed to interpret the group contrast. Any activity/protrusion measurements arising from the mechanism proposals require a separately agreed assay and should be distinguished from the basic motility pilot. Statistical models, uncertainty reporting and sample-size targets remain open.
narrative: This major results section will test whether the planned paired experimental system exhibits the migration behaviour motivating the theoretical work.
Its conclusions must follow the acquired observations, including null or opposing results. Simulation output and literature fits cannot fill this gap.
Agreement between increased polarity resistance or activity memory and migration persistence would support the proposed connection; causal attribution requires appropriate perturbations and controls.
measurements: Pending decisions include plating density, acquisition duration and cadence, field/condition throughput, tracking and exclusion rules, replicate structure, confirmation of WGD status, size quantification and the statistical analysis. The known throughput versus spatial/temporal resolution trade-off should be resolved by the pilot.

Mechanism validation can subsequently examine incumbent extent, early challenger growth, local loss/rebound, site fates and global activity-polarity correlation under characterized perturbations. These activity experiments are proposals alongside the theoretical mechanisms and are separate from the reserved motility-results contribution.
limitations: No pilot acquisition, sample size, effect estimate, significance claim or experimental outcome is supplied by the available evidence.

assets.page_title: S4. Migration-model adequacy and Hosny sensitivity

legend: The retained supplement explores signed-drift and leave-Hosny-out sensitivity within the declared OU hierarchy. Its fitted changes and descriptive-score profiles are conditional on the model and supplied summaries, not confidence intervals. Data-only identifiability, Xuan population-curve residuals and prior/pooling assumptions remain part of the adequacy assessment. Representative movie diagnostics are separate: acquisition timing is uncertain and nuclear appearance does not establish ploidy.

supplementary.title: Earlier supporting material: Gain and small-loss recovery: supporting evidence
legend: Calculated native input gain is separate from observed post-cue activity. The small-loss recovery contrast persists through stored finite trajectories but weakens with time; actual damage is only about0.22–0.285% of core activity, with no reporter calibration.
limitations: Small-loss assays are not the finite optical challenge or a universal stability measure.

supplementary.title: Earlier supporting material: Selected native pulse and causal controls
legend: WP L15 T20/T60 starts from the same basal state and illustrates withdrawal-dependent domain survival. Evolved interventions have endpoint- and cue-specific limits.
limitations: WP4× mobility passes orientation only at one dose; both conditions fail the stronger full-polarity-strength gate. Mobility is changed during cue and recovery.

supplementary.title: Earlier supporting material: Stationary-cue endpoint-vector alternative
text: An alternative view displays all 240 measured endpoint vectors on equal coordinate scales, with weak-resultant, overlap and finite-tail flags retained. It is available for discussion without replacing the complete withdrawal/retention map in the current review.
